policy.redirect_referer.reason: Go's net/http sets Referer on a followed redirect; simple_http does not. RFC 9110 §10.1.4 makes the field optional, and omitting it is the privacy-preserving choice.

policy.redirect_cross_origin.reason: Go's http.Client decides whether to forward Authorization/Cookie on a redirect by hostname only, ignoring the port; simple_http compares the full origin (scheme+host+port) per RFC 9110 §4.3.1 and strips them across a port change. The library is stricter and matches the origin boundary.

h3.status_204.reason: quic-go's HTTP/3 reference server emits Content-Length: 0 on a 204 (it fills Content-Length after the handler returns without excluding bodyless statuses). RFC 9110 §8.6 forbids Content-Length on a 204, and nghttp3 deliberately removes that field from the response header list (it tolerates the invalid value 0 on the wire but does not surface it), so simple_http reports framing=none while Go reports content-length. The C++ behavior is the RFC-aligned one.

raw.cl_te.reason: Go net/http accepts a request carrying both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding (TE wins); simple_http rejects the double framing with 400 per RFC 9112 §6.3 and as a request-smuggling defense.

raw.duplicate_cl.reason: Go net/http collapses/accepts duplicate identical Content-Length values; simple_http rejects duplicate Content-Length with 400 per RFC 9112 §6.3 (ambiguous framing / smuggling vector).

raw.obs_fold.reason: Go net/http accepts obsolete line folding in a header value; simple_http rejects it with 400. RFC 9112 §5.2 obsoletes obs-fold and permits rejecting it; rejecting avoids front-end/back-end smuggling splits.

body.request_trailers_h3.reason: C++ HTTP/3 request trailers are not exposed to handlers (documented limitation: only h1/h2 expose Request::trailers()); Go's quic-go server forwards them to r.Trailer, so /trailer-echo answers yes there and missing here. The case pins the limitation rather than hiding it.

h3raw.method_not_token.reason: nghttp3 rejects a non-token :method inside nghttp3_conn_read_stream2 with a connection-level NGHTTP3_ERR_MALFORMED_HTTP_HEADER, so C++ closes the QUIC connection; quic-go resets only the stream. RFC 9114 §4.1.2 asks for an H3_MESSAGE_ERROR stream error, so Go's granularity is closer to the RFC, but the decision is made by nghttp3, not by this library.

h3raw.method_empty.reason: Same nghttp3 connection-level MALFORMED_HTTP_HEADER path as h3raw.method_not_token: an empty :method is not a token (RFC 9110 §9), nghttp3 closes the connection, quic-go resets the stream.

h3raw.path_space.reason: nghttp3 treats a raw SP in :path as MALFORMED_HTTP_HEADER and closes the connection; quic-go accepts the request and the Go reference server answers 404. RFC 9113 §8.3.1 defines :path as the URI path/query, whose grammar excludes SP, so rejecting is RFC-aligned even though nghttp3 escalates to a connection error.

h3raw.path_backslash.reason: simple_http rejects DEL/backslash in :path as malformed (RFC 3986 path grammar excludes a raw backslash) and resets the stream; quic-go accepts it and answers 404. The C++ side is the stricter, RFC-aligned behaviour.

h3raw.authority_space.reason: nghttp3 closes the connection for SP in :authority; quic-go accepts it. The authority production (RFC 3986 §3.2) excludes SP, so the C++ rejection is correct, only its granularity is nghttp3's.

h3raw.header_uppercase.reason: Both reject an uppercase field name, as RFC 9113 §8.2.1 and RFC 9114 §4.2 require, but nghttp3 surfaces it as a connection error while quic-go resets the stream. The difference is nghttp3's error classification.

h3raw.header_separator.reason: nghttp3 drops a regular field whose name is not a token (e.g. `x(y`) and lets the request through, so C++ answers 200; quic-go treats it as malformed and resets the stream. RFC 9110 §5.1 defines field-name = token and RFC 9114 §4.1.2 treats an invalid field as malformed, so Go is closer to the RFC; nghttp3 does not hand the field to the application, which is why the library's own token check cannot fire.
